units.translation: But now I fear that the swift-footed Fury may fulfill it.
I would not fear any adornment of a man.
Who, without fearing, will stand against a boastful man?
Did you fear any of the absent rulers?
Fearing the wrath of other necessities (thus Bothius for 'of another necessity') or of someone (thus from the copy for 'of no one')?
And the sea-born plague that shakes the earth, the trident, the spear of Poseidon, scatters it.
I see this trident, a sign of the god.
Fearing these tridents and the reverence of the gods.
Into ten groups of thirty ships.

A metaphor taken from the wrestling school, in which athletes who have been thrown three times are said to be τριαχθῆναι [to be thrice thrown] or ἀποτριαχθῆναι [to be completely thrice thrown]: see Thes. vol. 7 p. 2409. Aeschylus said ἀτρίακτον ἄταν [unconquerable ruin] in Ch. 339, which cannot be overcome.
He is gone, having met with a victor.
where the scholiast says: ὡς τῶν οἴκων φυγόντων τὰς συντριβὰς τῶν οἴκων [as if the houses had escaped the shatterings of the houses].

The scholiast wrongly explains: τὸν συντρίψαντά μου ταῖς ἐπιμελείαις τὴν ψυχήν [the one who has crushed my soul with cares]. More correctly Hemsterhuis in Thes. vol. 7 p. 2412 took it as said for διατριβήν [pastime], i.e., delight.
where the scholiast says: διαγωγήν, διήγησιν ἀξίαν ἔχει τὸ εἰπεῖν [the saying has a worthy pastime and narrative].
In a life of changing fortune and wear.
Raise a cry of joy, O house of our masters, for the escape from evils and the wear of possessions.
And dear Orestes, the delight of my soul.
To lament and bewail one's fortunes here, where one is likely to receive tears from the hearers, has a worthy pastime.
as if the houses had escaped the shatterings of the houses
the one who has crushed my soul with cares
the saying has a worthy pastime and narrative
where the scholiast explains it by διατριβή [pastime]
And to Harmonia has been given the fate of Aphrodite's whisperings and the paths of loves.
By rubbing and by blows it becomes dark and solid.
Making the time long again, they wore down the flower of the Argives by rubbing.

In the same meaning τρίβεσθαι [to be rubbed] is taken by the interpreters at Eum. 195: λέοντος ἄντρον αἱματορρόφου οἰκεῖν τοιαύτας εἰκὸς, οὐ χρηστηρίοις ἐν τοῖσδε πλησίοισι (πλουσίοισι Pauwius) τρίβεσθαι μύσος [it is likely that such creatures dwell in the den of a blood-drinking lion, not that pollution is rubbed off in these nearby (wealthy, Pauwius) oracles], as if μύσος [pollution] were said for μύσος οὔσας [being pollution], which is hardly probable. The scholiast understood what should have been said, who took it as μύσος προστρίβεσθαι [pollution to be rubbed upon].
To wear out another race with murderous deaths.
Indeed, I have no leisure to spend on this foreign matter (thus Musgrave for 'this').
it is likely that such creatures dwell in the den of a blood-drinking lion, not that pollution is rubbed off in these nearby (wealthy, Pauwius) oracles
A very old tale speaks these things.
